title: Dodds identifies Oliver records; Jimmie Noone in Chicago and Los Angeles
summary: Dodds's poverty and his identifications of personnel on Oliver records; then Jimmie Noone's later career and death.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: I heard that song as a white religious piece.

Really? A religious group. The oldest record I ever came across was an old Paramount which wasn't anything very jazzy, you might say. a quartet. You know, a sacred quartet. But anyway, to get back to Dodds, I was surprised then, of course, that to me he was somebody famous. Anybody on the Louis Hot Five would be a famous musician. And he even had a sign out in the front. I was surprised that that was in the first big popularity cycle of Benny Goodman had just made his big hit out in California at the Palladium or someplace and starting to make these Victor records and the swing was just coming on. It was just a big rage. And Benny Goodman even that summer had become known as the world's greatest clarinetist. So they probably got the idea from that. They had this sign out on the little painted, hand-painted sign out in front, Johnny Dodds, the world's greatest clarinetist. I was sort of surprised to see that. But inside, he was probably, it wasn't a union job, I'm sure. Because all the time I knew him in New York, he was playing non-union jobs. He might have been a member of the union even up until the last because he made some records in 1938. But these were little three-dollar-a-night jobs or so, anything he could get. Sometime they'd, I think baby, that'll be in some of the baby notes that I have, they'd play for, oh, anything they could get maybe the cafe owner or the saloon owner, if they had a restaurant, would give them a bag of food or something like that. They'd even play for things like that during the break. Things were really bad and that's about how bad it was there when Johnny Dodds was playing this little trio job. So he invited me to his home next day. At that time, I was one of these dyed-in-the-wool record collectors, you know, which was pretty, well, they were a pretty bad set, including me, you know. I mean, all the interest in the way was collecting records like stamps, although, of course, I did like the music. I'm not trying to say it was better than the other collectors, but a lot of the collectors, unfortunately, just collect them like stamps. But I went to his house, of course, armed with a whole big box of records I'd picked up. I remember I'd been in Buffalo a couple nights before and picked up some of the Oliver Columbia records, which we found now definitely have Jimmy Noon on. So I took all the Oliver records I had with me, including the Jeanettes and O.K.'s, and he'd say, oh yes, that's me identifying, told who else was in the band, which in general checked with other people. Some of those Oliver records have never been definitely established about the bass, whether it's Bill Johnson on the bass or whether there's a bass sax on there played by some Jackson or, because you couldn't hear the bass anyway, much below middle C didn't record very well anyway. Bill Johnson sometimes played banjo. But anyway, when we got to the Columbia records, those four sides on Columbia like Camp Meeting Blues and the New Arlene Stomp and another tune that Piku has his name on some of those too, P. Rohn. Dodds would say, it's not me, the clarinet. I'd say, have any ideas of Jimmy Noon? I don't know, it's not me. It seemed, not that he was just self-centered or anything, but if it wasn't Johnny, he wouldn't even venture a guess as to who it was. He'd say, it's not me. And he did at least identify the ones he was on, which we knew pretty well then anyway, but at least I did confirm some of those personnels, which at that time weren't really generally known. But that was one of my main interests, not only just to hear him, but to try to establish those personnels and it was a record collecting trip that I was on. I also got to meet, I'll write up those other notes a little bit fuller than I have even in my other notebook about Dodds. And I also went to see Jimmy Noon about that time and especially the next year or two, around 37 and 38 I remember. I remember one funny thing I always have to laugh at, he was always so heavy, he's really fat. At one time he hadn't been working for a long time, which is the truth, he was in a bad shape financially, but I remember him saying, I'm starving to death, I'm just starving to death. And yet he was, must have weighed 250 or more. He wasn't very tall, so he maybe didn't weigh so much. But he always had usually a group with just a piano, maybe three or four players, no really organized. One year I did hear him in a place called Platinum Club where he had about an eight or nine piece band, might have been ten piece. Played for floor shows and all.

Chicago. Chicago. Then later he went to Los Angeles and died out there and made some records with Ori, or maybe not records, he made some radio appearances for Orson Welles, which he only really knew Arlene's band, type band he played with, say six or seven pieces for many years. He made them for this group with Mud Carey and Zutty Singleton as the drummer. So I'll hunt up some of those noon notes which are very sketchy too, very unfortunately. Very little is known about his life. I mentioned about Norwood Williams. You might look up some notes on him right now if I can find them. He had been the guitar player in the original trio band that had left here probably around 1914. According to some of the books, including Jazzmen, that band had left here in 1912. But a few of them had been out there including Dink Johnson and maybe Bill Johnson had a little trio at first as far as I can understand out in Los Angeles. But the whole band with Keppard and all those pictures that are taken probably weren't really taken maybe as early as 1912. It might have been as late as 1914. If we could get somebody in Los Angeles to go over those newspapers we could find out more about it because they played for some of the prize fights out there.
